No. There is a 38-vertex median graph  $G$  with
$$\boxed{\beta _2(G)=21<22\le SF_2(G).}$$
The graph is a  $4\times4\times2$  rectangular prism with six pendant vertices attached. Below are its complete adjacency list, an explicit inclusion-minimal forming set of size  $22$ , all deletion witnesses, a direct median proof, and a proof that its dissociation number is exactly  $21$ .This disproves the universal median-graph claim. It does not refute the equality for rectangular grids themselves.1. ConstructionLet
$$B=P_4\square P_4\square K_2,$$
with coordinates
$$V(B)=\{(x,y,z):x,y\in\{0,1,2,3\},\ z\in\{0,1\}\}.$$
Two vertices are adjacent exactly when their Manhattan distance is one.Write
$$C=\{(0,0),(3,0),(0,3)\},
\qquad
D=\{(x,y,0):(x,y)\in C\}.$$
At each of the three vertices in  $D$ , attach two pendant leaves. Let  $L$  be the set of these six leaves, and let  $G$  be the resulting graph. Thus
$$|V(G)|=32+6=38.$$
The three points of  $C$  have pairwise distances
$$3,\quad 3,\quad 6$$
in  $P_4\square P_4$ . Consequently:They are pairwise nonadjacent.Every grid vertex has at most one neighbour in  $C$ .These two properties will give the formation and minimality certificates.2. Direct proof that  $G$  is medianFirst,  $B$  is median directly from its distance formula:
$$d_B\bigl((x,y,z),(x',y',z')\bigr)
=|x-x'|+|y-y'|+|z-z'|.$$
Its intervals are coordinate boxes. Therefore the unique median of three vertices is obtained by taking the ordinary median in each coordinate.Now project every pendant leaf to its attachment vertex in  $B$ , and leave every vertex of  $B$  fixed. Denote this projection by  $\pi$ .For two distinct vertices  $a,b\in V(G)$ ,
$$I_G(a,b)\cap V(B)=I_B\bigl(\pi(a),\pi(b)\bigr).$$
Indeed, a shortest path from a pendant vertex must first traverse its unique incident edge; after that, shortest paths run inside  $B$ .For a triple of distinct vertices, no pendant vertex can be a median: a pendant vertex cannot lie on a shortest path between two other vertices. Thus any median must lie in  $B$ , where the three interval conditions reduce to those for the three projected vertices. Their coordinatewise median is the unique solution. Triples with a repeated vertex have that repeated vertex as their unique median.Hence  $G$  is a finite connected median graph under the definition in the question.3. A minimal forming set of size  $22$ Define
$$S_L=\{(x,y,0):(x,y)\notin C\},$$

$$S_U=\{(x,y,1):(x,y)\in C\},$$
and
$$S=S_L\cup S_U\cup L.$$
Its size is
$$|S|=13+3+6=22.$$
Activity inside  $G[S]$ Every vertex of the base grid  $P_4\square P_4$  has degree at least two. A vertex outside  $C$  has at most one neighbour in  $C$ , so every vertex in  $S_L$  has at least one neighbour in  $S_L$ . Thus every vertex of  $S_L$  is active.In contrast, every vertex of  $S_U$  is isolated in  $G[S]$ : its lower mate belongs to  $D$ , hence is outside  $S$ , and the three positions in  $C$  are pairwise nonadjacent.Every leaf in  $L$  is also isolated in  $G[S]$ , since its attachment vertex belongs to  $D$ .FormationThere are exactly two types of outside vertices.Outside vertexFormation certificateA lower vertex in  $D$ Its two pendant neighbours belong to  $S$ .An upper vertex  $(x,y,1)$  with  $(x,y)\notin C$ Its lower neighbour  $(x,y,0)$  belongs to  $S_L$  and is active.Thus  $S$  satisfies precisely the non-induced  $K_{1,2}$  formation criterion in the question.Every deletion failsHere are witnesses for every selected vertex.Delete  $s=(x,y,0)\in S_L$ .Use its upper mate
$$w_s=(x,y,1)$$
as the witness. This vertex was already outside  $S$ .After deleting  $s$ , its remaining selected neighbours can only be upper copies of neighbours of  $(x,y)$  in  $C$ . There is at most one such neighbour. If present, it belongs to  $S_U$  and remains isolated in the selected subgraph.Therefore  $w_s$  has either no selected neighbour or exactly one isolated selected neighbour. It is not formed.Delete  $s\in S_U$ .The deleted vertex itself is now outside. It has no selected neighbour, because it was isolated in  $G[S]$ . Thus it is not formed.Delete  $s\in L$ .Again, the deleted vertex itself is the witness. Its unique neighbour belongs to  $D$ , which is outside  $S$ , so it has no selected neighbour.The thirteen upper-mate witnesses are distinct. The other nine witnesses are the deleted vertices themselves.Finally, formation is upward monotone: a forming set remains forming when more vertices are selected. Hence failure of every single-vertex deletion proves inclusion-minimality. We have established
$$\boxed{SF_2(G)\ge22.}$$
4. The key dissociation calculationLet
$$F=B-D$$
be the induced subgraph obtained by removing the three lower corner vertices, without adding any leaves.I will prove
$$\boxed{\beta_2(F)=15.}$$
The proof uses four cube blocks and a complete, elementary classification of their maximum dissociation sets.4.1. Dissociation sets of size four in  $Q_3$ Every dissociation set in  $Q_3$  has size at most four: partition the cube into two square faces, each of which contains at most two selected vertices.In local coordinates  $(u,v,w)\in\{0,1\}^3$ , every size-four dissociation set has exactly one of the following forms. All equations in this subsection are modulo two.TypeSelected vertices, for a phase  $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$  $P$  $u+v+w=\varepsilon$  $X$  $v+w=\varepsilon$  $Y$  $u+w=\varepsilon$  $Z$  $u+v=\varepsilon$ Here type  $P$  is independent. Each of types  $X,Y,Z$  consists of two parallel edges, so every selected vertex already has one selected neighbour inside the cube.Proof of completeness. If a size-four dissociation set contains an edge, the endpoints exclude their four other cube neighbours. The only two remaining available vertices form the opposite parallel edge. This gives type  $X$ ,  $Y$ , or  $Z$ , according to the edge direction.Otherwise the set is independent. Its four vertices have twelve incident edges, accounting for all twelve cube edges. Its complement is therefore also independent. Since the cube is connected, this is its usual bipartition, giving type  $P$ . ∎4.2. Partition the prism into four cubesPartition  $B$  into the disjoint induced cubes
$$B_{ij}
=
\{(2i+u,2j+v,w):u,v,w\in\{0,1\}\},
\qquad i,j\in\{0,1\}.$$
Every dissociation set in  $B$ , and therefore in  $F$ , has size at most
$$4+4+4+4=16.$$
Suppose, toward a contradiction, that  $I\subseteq V(F)$  is a dissociation set of size  $16$ . Then it selects exactly four vertices in each cube  $B_{ij}$ . No choice of four block patterns avoids the three deleted verticesWe exhaust all possibilities.Case 1: Some block has type  $Z$ .Across either boundary direction, its neighbour must also have type  $Z$  with the same phase. Hence all four blocks have type  $Z$  and a common phase.Avoiding  $(0,0,0)$  requires this phase to be  $1$ , since its local value of  $u+v$  is  $0$ . Contradiction.Case 2: Some block has type  $X$ .Across a  $y$ -boundary, an  $X$  block can only meet another  $X$  block, with the same phase. The contradiction now uses the two omitted vertices
$$(0,0,0),\qquad (3,0,0).$$
Case 4: All four blocks have type  $P$ .Avoiding the three omitted vertices forces
$$\varepsilon_{00}=1,\qquad
\varepsilon_{10}=0,\qquad
\varepsilon_{01}=0.$$
But then all three vertices
$$(1,1,1),\qquad (2,1,1),\qquad (1,2,1)$$

This gives selected degree at least two, a contradiction.All possibilities have been excluded. Therefore
$$\beta_2(F)\le15.$$
For the reverse inequality, take the even-parity vertices of  $B$ ,
$$x+y+z\equiv0\pmod2,$$
except  $(0,0,0)$ . This is an independent set of size  $15$  contained in  $F$ : the other two removed vertices have odd parity.Thus
$$\boxed{\beta_2(F)=15.}$$
5. Exact dissociation number of  $G$ Let  $A$  be any dissociation set of  $G$ .If an attachment vertex  $d\in D$  belongs to  $A$ , at most one of its two pendant leaves can also belong to  $A$ . Replace  $d$  and any selected leaf at  $d$  by both pendant leaves.This operation:Never decreases cardinality.Preserves maximum induced degree at most one.Can only remove selected adjacencies elsewhere.Perform it at every selected attachment vertex, and then add any still-missing pendant leaves. The resulting dissociation set contains all six leaves and no vertex of  $D$ . Its remaining vertices form a dissociation set of  $F$ . Hence
$$|A|\le6+\beta_2(F)=21.$$
Conversely, the fifteen-vertex independent set from the preceding section, together with all six leaves, is independent in  $G$ . Therefore
$$\boxed{\beta_2(G)=21.}$$
Together with the minimal forming set constructed above, this proves
$$\boxed{\beta_2(G)=21<22\le SF_2(G).}$$
An exact upper bound on  $SF_2(G)$  is not needed for this strict separation, and none is being asserted here.6. Complete adjacency list and numeric certificatesNumber the prism vertices by

7. Consequences for rectangular gridsThe example proves that medianity alone cannot supply the desired  $SF_2\le\beta_2$  theorem.It also identifies a specific failure of preservation: the underlying prism
$$B=(P_4\square P_4)\square K_2$$
satisfies your prism equality, with
$$SF_2(B)=\beta_2(B)=16.$$
Attaching the six pendant vertices preserves medianity but destroys that equality.The resulting graph is not a rectangular grid  $P_m\square P_n$ . It has pendant vertices and vertices of degree five. More generally, it is not any Cartesian product of paths: a product with at least two nontrivial factors has minimum degree at least two, while a product with only one nontrivial factor is a path.Thus this counterexample rules out the universal median-graph route, while leaving the rectangular-grid  $SF_2/\beta_2$  question—and the additional equality involving  $\psi_\square$ —unresolved by this construction.
